<div class="project-content">

<p class="lede-para">
  A deliberately small project with a deliberate purpose: build the database layer by hand. No ORM, no framework —
  just Java, JDBC, and a PostgreSQL schema I designed myself, so that every query and every connection is something I
  had to reason about.
</p>

<h2>Schema design</h2>

<ul>
  <li>Designed a PostgreSQL <code>tasks</code> table with columns for task ID, name, description, due date and status.</li>
  <li>Chose types and constraints up front rather than letting a migration tool decide them.</li>
</ul>

<h2>JDBC integration</h2>

<ul>
  <li>Established the JDBC connection and wrote the SQL for insert, select, update and delete directly.</li>
  <li>Used <strong>prepared statements throughout</strong> — parameterized queries, so user input never reaches the
  database as concatenated SQL. This is the whole reason to write the layer by hand: SQL injection stops being an
  abstract lesson.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Application</h2>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Add</strong> a task with name, description, due date and status.</li>
  <li><strong>View</strong> every task currently persisted.</li>
  <li><strong>Update</strong> a task's name or status.</li>
  <li><strong>Delete</strong> a task permanently.</li>
  <li>Wrapped in a console interface that prompts for each operation.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Where it goes next</h2>

<p>
  The natural extensions are user authentication, filtering and sorting on the query side, and a real front end. The
  backend is already structured so that swapping the console for an HTTP layer would not require rewriting the data
  access code.
</p>
